network.overall_strategy: This network traces ten experimentally supported and geochemically plausible pathways to glycine, integrating Strecker-type aldehyde–cyanide chemistry; cyanosulfidic photochemistry; glyoxylate and mineral-driven protometabolic routes; surface and hydrothermal hydrolysis of precursor pools; and secondary impact/extraterrestrial delivery. Routes are organized according to their distinct C, N, and energy sources, as justified by the literature, and include key intermediates such as aminoacetonitrile, glycinamide, glyoxylate imine, N-oxalylglycine, and hydantoin. Environmental and concentration/compatibility constraints are respected throughout.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde + Ammonia + HCN Strecker Synthesis

conditions.other: Requires millimolar to high-millimolar reactant concentrations

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of cyanide to imine formed from formaldehyde and ammonia yields aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The classical Strecker amino acid synthesis is well established experimentally and is central to many prebiotic amino acid experiments, including Miller's and Schlesinger's. No mineral catalyst is required (Miller, 1957; Schlesinger & Miller, 1983; Johnson et al., 2008).

reactions.name: Aminoacetonitrile Hydrolysis to Glycinamide

conditions.other: Mildly acidic or neutral pH, hydrolysis requires heat or extended time

reactions.mechanism: Stepwise hydrolysis of the nitrile group to amide.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated in acidic or prolonged aqueous conditions following Strecker/HCN chemistry (Miller, 1957; Oró & Kamat, 1961; Schlesinger & Miller, 1983).

reactions.name: Glycinamide Hydrolysis to Glycine

conditions.other: Can occur on mineral surfaces or in water during hydrolysis step

reactions.mechanism: Amide hydrolysis to carboxyl group, forming glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Final conversion in the Strecker sequence; confirmed experimentally as the main glycine liberation step (Miller, 1957; Schlesinger & Miller, 1983).

reactions.name: HCN Addition to Formaldehyde (Glycolonitrile Formation)

conditions.other: Favored in cold, moderately concentrated solutions

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide nucleophilic attack on formaldehyde forms glycolonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Observed as a key condensation product and precursor to Strecker network (Miller, 1957; Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Ammoniation of Glycolonitrile to Aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Can proceed with or without minerals

reactions.mechanism: Amination/nucleophilic attack of ammonia on glycolonitrile converts the hydroxyl to an amino group, yielding aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Established in cyanide/aldehyde/ammonia systems; direct evidence from atmospheric and cyanosulfidic prebiotic experiments (Patel et al., 2015; Schlesinger & Miller, 1983).

reactions.name: Aza-Cannizzaro Disproportionation (Glyoxylate + Ammonia)

conditions.other: Strongly concentration-dependent; efficient above ~0.25M glyoxylate, pH 7-10

reactions.mechanism: Imine/hemiaminal intermediate forms; internal hydride transfer yields glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Clean, experimentally demonstrated non-cyanide glycine formation in concentrated ammonium/glyoxylate solutions (Jarois et al., 2024).

reactions.name: FeS/Fe⁰-Catalyzed Glyoxylate Reductive Amination
reactions.mechanism: Glyoxylate reacts with ammonia to form imine; mineral Fe(II)/Fe(0) supplies electrons to reduce imine to glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by laboratory experiments directly connecting FeS-Fe⁰ systems to glycine synthesis from glyoxylate and NH3 (Kitadai et al., 2019).

reactions.name: Nitrate Reduction Coupled Glyoxylate Reductive Amination (Brucite)
reactions.mechanism: Fe(II) reduces nitrate to ammonia, which condenses with glyoxylate; further reduction gives glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Laboratory experiments confirm coupling of nitrate reduction and glycine formation; majority of glycine forms bound to mineral phase (Chimiak et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Bucherer–Bergs Reaction (Glyoxylate + Ammonia + Cyanide)

conditions.other: Often heated, works without added catalysts

reactions.mechanism: Glyoxylate, cyanide and ammonia react to form hydantoin intermediates.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated for α-ketoacids conversion to amino acids with hydantoin intermediates; glycine is major product after hydrolysis (Pulletikurti et al., 2022).

reactions.name: Hydantoin Hydrolysis to Glycine

conditions.other: Hydrolysis promoted by heating, acid/base catalysts or wet-dry cycles

reactions.mechanism: Ring-opening of hydantoin and loss of ammonia yields glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Robustly observed in heated Bucherer–Bergs systems and geochemical experiments, precursor to glycine (Pulletikurti et al., 2022).

reactions.name: Formaldehyde + Hydroxylamine to Formaldoxime
reactions.mechanism: Condensation of formaldehyde and hydroxylamine yields formaldoxime.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated in metal-rich aqueous solutions; forms important intermediate for downstream glycine formation (Oró et al., 1959).

reactions.name: Formaldoxime Chemistry to Aminoacetonitrile/Glycinamide
reactions.mechanism: C–N rearrangement and elimination of water yields aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Observed in formaldehyde/hydroxylamine/ammonia experiments; glycinamide and aminoacetonitrile are dominant non-hydrolyzed products (Kamaluddin et al., 1979; Oró et al., 1959).

reactions.name: Formaldehyde + Ammonia Polymerization (non-cyanide route)

conditions.other: Requires wet-dry, heating cycles; hydrolysis liberates glycine

reactions.mechanism: Thermal condensation yields a complex N-organic polymer that upon hydrolysis gives glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally confirmed: heat treatment of formaldehyde and ammonia gives hydrolyzable polymer with glycine as predominant amino acid; mechanism not fully resolved, but robust (Fox & Windsor, 1970).

reactions.name: Impact Shock of Formic Acid and Ammonium Nitrate to Glycine
reactions.mechanism: Mechanical/thermal shock drives bond rearrangement; hydrolysis liberates glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Directly observed in simulated ocean-impact shock experiments; yields are low but mechanistically relevant (Suzuki et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Ethanolamine Oxidation to Aminoacetaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted dehydrogenation, then oxidation, yields aminoacetaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally confirmed in alkaline, metal-rich hydrothermal conditions; conversion tightly dependent on co-located metals and high ethanolamine concentration (Zhang et al., 2017).

reactions.name: Aminoacetaldehyde Oxidation to Glycine
reactions.mechanism: Disproportionation or direct oxidation (possibly metal catalyzed) completes conversion of aldehyde to carboxyl group, yielding glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Seamless sequence from ethanolamine to glycine observed experimentally, with aminoacetaldehyde as a dominantly detected intermediate (Zhang et al., 2017).

reactions.name: N-oxalylglycine Hydrolysis to Glycine

conditions.other: Often executed in acid (pH 1-2) or with strong hydrolysis

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis breaks N-acyl bond, liberating free glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Laboratory demonstration of glyoxylate–ammonia condensation forming N-oxalylglycine, which hydrolyzes to glycine (Yanagawa et al., 1984).

reactions.name: Glyoxylate + Ammonia Condensation to N-oxalylglycine
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic acyl substitution of glyoxylate by ammonia forms N-oxalylglycine.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally supported as non-reductive, non-cyanide path to bound glycine precursor (Yanagawa et al., 1984).

pathways.name: Surface Strecker (Classical Miller–Urey)
pathways.description: Formaldehyde, ammonia and HCN combine in an aqueous surface environment to form aminoacetonitrile, followed by stepwise hydrolysis to glycinamide and then glycine.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic–Glycolonitrile Branch
pathways.description: Formaldehyde and HCN generate glycolonitrile, which is ammoniated to aminoacetonitrile and proceeds via Strecker hydrolysis to glycine.

pathways.name: Non-Cyanide Glyoxylate Aza-Cannizzaro Reaction
pathways.description: Glyoxylate undergoes hydride transfer in the presence of concentrated ammonia (or ammonium) directly to glycine in aqueous surface/evaporite settings.

pathways.name: Alkaline Hydrothermal FeS–Fe⁰ Reductive Amination
pathways.description: Hydrothermally derived glyoxylate reacts with ammonia over reduced iron minerals, directly producing glycine without cyanide.

pathways.name: Nitrate–Ferroan Brucite System
pathways.description: Surface nitrate is reduced by Fe(II) in ferroan brucite, generating ammonia in situ for condensation with glyoxylate and subsequent reduction to glycine.

pathways.name: Bucherer–Bergs Hydantoin Pathway
pathways.description: Glyoxylate, cyanide and ammonia generate hydantoin, which upon hydrolysis yields glycine.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde–Hydroxylamine Route to Aminoacetonitrile
pathways.description: Formaldehyde reacts with hydroxylamine to form formaldoxime, which rearranges (with ammonia) to aminoacetonitrile before hydrolysis to glycine.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde–Ammonia Polymer Route
pathways.description: Heating formaldehyde and ammonia yields a polymer that liberates glycine upon hydrolysis; no externally supplied cyanide is required.

pathways.name: Impact Shock (Formic Acid + Ammonium Nitrate)
pathways.description: Shock-processing of formic acid with ammonium nitrate produces glycine in dilute aqueous environments via high temperature and pressure.

pathways.name: Ethanolamine Oxidation Route
pathways.description: Ethanolamine, supplied in a hydrothermal setting, is oxidized by metals to aminoacetaldehyde, which is then further oxidized/disproportionated to glycine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Classical Strecker network has the right sequence and is well-founded in prebiotic chemistry but every reaction is unbalanced, notably the final hydrolysis steps (rxn_003) which appear to gain N and H inconsistently. Environmental fit is strong, and chemistry is literature-aligned, but mass conservation and possible mechanism errors lower chemical feasibility and target confidence.
suggestions: Fix atom/charge balance for all steps, clarify hydrolysis stoichiometry, ensure each step has explicit side products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanosulfidic–glycolonitrile route is realistic and consistent with Patel et al. (2015). However, all reactions in the route are unbalanced (missing H2O, O, etc.), particularly the hydrolysis to glycine. Chemistry and steps are defensible but network needs element conservation and explicit side products to support validity.
suggestions: Add missing water and/or O-containing species to balance equations, clarify mechanistic steps, check N and H handling in all hydrolyses.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Aza-Cannizzaro route is literature-backed, experimentally supported and environmentally sound for concentrated surface settings. However, the reaction as written is unbalanced (O +1) and may miss side products (e.g., oxamic acid). Chemistry otherwise plausible and mechanism is addressed, but stoichiometry needs adjustment.
suggestions: Add missing side products (e.g., oxamate/oxamic acid), ensure atom balance, clarify aqueous/ionic states if relevant.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: FeS/Fe⁰-catalyzed reductive amination fits Kitadai et al. and is a valid prebiotic hydrothermal step. The overall chemical step is plausible, but the reaction is unbalanced (O +1) as written, and potentially needs explicit H2/H2O handling. Still, chemistry and environment are well-linked.
suggestions: Balance the reaction fully; include side products such as water, show redox equivalents transferred, clarify FeS role.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Nitrate reduction with brucite is based on Chimiak et al., but this reaction is unbalanced both in mass and charge, and no way to balance with small molecules. Chemistry is plausible and references support path, but net chemistry as written is not physically valid.
suggestions: Balance N and O atoms, specify reduction products (e.g., NH3 formation, Fe oxidation state transitions), ensure charge conservation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Bucherer–Bergs reaction chain (to hydantoin and glycine) is correct in concept and matches literature, but both reactions are unbalanced—C and N are mismatched and no single set of common side products fixes the equations. Chemistry is literature-aligned but network needs precise reaction stoichiometry and intermediate handling.
suggestions: Balance equations, assign all carbon sources and sinks, clarify decarboxylation/hydrolysis byproducts, correct for N and H count discrepancies.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The formaldehyde–hydroxylamine pathway is literature-consistent (Oró et al.) and mostly plausible but several reactions (notably hydrolyses) are unbalanced. The initial steps are chemically solid, but later hydrolysis to glycine is in the same problematic form as Strecker. Needs consistent atom/charge stoichiometry.
suggestions: Correct mass/charge conservation in all steps, ensure formaldoxime and precursor conversion is explicit, add water or other correctants as needed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Classical formaldehyde + ammonia yields glycine after hydrolysis (Fox & Windsor) but the reaction is unbalanced—missing a carbon unit and short of H and O. Chemistry is plausible in general, but not as written. Mechanism and required hydrolysis are under-specified.
suggestions: Balance the equation, specify hydrolysis byproducts, clarify chemical structure of the intermediate polymer if relevant.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Impact shock chemistry is supported by literature (Suzuki et al.) but reaction is unbalanced in elements and no obvious correction with simple species. Chemistry is plausible for impact, but representative as a precursor generation, not clean single-step glycine synthesis.
suggestions: Balance atom and charge, specify nitrogen handling, clarify any intermediates or side products, consider compatibility with both shock and aqueous media.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ethanolamine oxidation route follows the Zhang et al. hydrothermal experiment; chemical steps are individually plausible but both reactions are unbalanced (loss of H2 or requirement for O2 unaccounted). Valid route but needs full redox and atom tracking.
suggestions: Balance all equations, add lost H2 for dehydrogenation, clarify oxidant for glycine formation, ensure oxygen source is specified.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Glyoxylate to N-oxalylglycine and hydrolysis branch matches Yanagawa et al., but both reactions are unbalanced (C, N, O, H mismatch). Chemically justified as a route, but equations must account for all mass and charge properly. Lack of acid hydrolysis step detail limits target confidence.
suggestions: Add explicit side products (CO2, H2O), confirm stoichiometry, correct acid hydrolysis step as needed for atom conservation.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network strongly integrates the best-established experimental routes to glycine and demonstrates broad chemical knowledge, with nearly all plausible prebiotic pathways present. However, every assessed reaction except possibly the initial formaloxime step is unbalanced by element or charge, and many hydrolyses add or lose atoms without clear source or sink. This is a critical violation for network validity, not merely a literature annotation gap. Environmental consistency, strategy, and pathway coherence are otherwise good, and the routes match the literature very well including acknowledgement of concentration, catalysis, and hydrolysis boundary issues. To achieve approval, all reactions must be fully balanced, small molecule byproducts or cosubstrates must be inserted, and ambiguous steps clarified. The chemistry as written suggests the network is a highly literate summary of current prebiotic possibilities, but formal accuracy requires complete mass/charge conservation.
